Withstood
with-STOOD
v. (past t. and past part.)
From withstand, Saxon withstandan — with in its older sense of against, and stand. Webster 1828: opposed; resisted, either with physical or moral means. Literally, to stand against.

Biblical Definition

Withstood means stood against, and Scripture gives four instances that between them cover almost every legitimate and illegitimate form of resistance. Paul withstood an apostle publicly and gives his reason in the same breath: But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed (Galatians 2:11) — not for a doctrinal statement Peter had made but for a table he had withdrawn from, because the gospel was at stake in the practice. Priests withstood a king who had taken a censer into the temple: they withstood Uzziah the king, and said unto him, It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests (2 Chronicles 26:18), and God struck him with leprosy on the spot. An angel reports being withstood in the unseen realm: the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me (Daniel 10:13) — three weeks of Daniel’s praying while an answer was delayed by a conflict he could not see. And Paul names the pattern of resistance to truth itself: as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth: men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith (2 Timothy 3:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WITHSTOOD as the past tense and participle of WITHSTAND: opposed; resisted; stood against, either by physical force or by argument and remonstrance.

expand to see more

WITHSTOOD, pret. and pp. of WITHSTAND — Opposed; resisted; stood in opposition to.

WITHSTAND, v.t. — To oppose; to resist, either with physical or moral force.

To stand against; to hold out against; as, to withstand an assault or a temptation.

To resist by argument, remonstrance, or open rebuke, as one man withstanding another to the face.

From with, in the old sense of against, and stand; compare withhold and withdraw.

Key Scripture

Galatians 2:11 — "But when Peter was come to Antioch, I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed."

2 Chronicles 26:18 — "And they withstood Uzziah the king, and said unto him, It appertaineth not unto thee, Uzziah, to burn incense unto the LORD, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, that are consecrated to burn incense: go out of the sanctuary; for thou hast trespassed; neither shall it be for thine honour from the LORD God."

Daniel 10:13 — "But the prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days: but, lo, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me; and I remained there with the kings of Persia."

2 Timothy 3:8 — "Now as Jannes and Jambres withstood Moses, so do these also resist the truth: men of corrupt minds, reprobate concerning the faith."

Modern Corruption

Galatians 2:11 records one apostle publicly rebuking another over conduct, and both the deference that will not confront a leader and the online habit of confronting everyone about everything mistake what Paul actually did.

expand to see more

The circumstances are worth noting because they bound the example. Peter had eaten with Gentiles and then withdrew when men came from James, and other Jews and even Barnabas were carried away with his dissimulation. Paul’s charge is that they walked not uprightly according to the truth of the gospel. So the rebuke was public because the sin was public and its effect was spreading; it was over an action, not a suspicion; it concerned the gospel itself, not a preference; and it was delivered face to face by a man of equal standing. Every one of those features is usually missing from the modern confrontation, which is typically about an inference, delivered to an audience rather than a face, and concerning a matter of taste. Matthew 18 governs private offences; Galatians 2 governs public ones. Neither authorises what social media has made ordinary.

2 Chronicles 26:18 and Daniel 10:13 show two other kinds. Azariah and eighty priests withstood a king at the height of his success — Uzziah had built towers, dug wells, and made engines of war, and Scripture says when he was strong, his heart was lifted up to his destruction. Withstanding him was dangerous, and they did it anyway, on the ground of what appertained to whom. Daniel’s case is the one that should shape a believer’s prayers: he had been fasting three weeks with no answer, and the angel says the answer left on the first day and was withstood. Delay is not always refusal, and what delays it may be nothing the praying man could have known about.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek anthistemi (G436), to set oneself against, to withstand; Hebrew amad al, to stand against; Greek antitasso (G498), to arrange in battle against; histemi (G2476), to stand.

expand to see more

Greek anthistemi (G436) — to stand against, to resist; I withstood him to the face (Galatians 2:11) and Resist the devil (James 4:7).

Greek antitasso (G498) — to set in battle array against; God resisteth the proud (James 4:6).

Greek histemi (G2476) — to stand; the root of the whole family, and of having done all, to stand (Ephesians 6:13).

Hebrew amad (H5975) — to stand, to take a stand; the priests standing against Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:18).

Aramaic sar — prince; the prince of the kingdom of Persia (Daniel 10:13), a spiritual power over a nation.

Usage

"I withstood him to the face, because he was to be blamed (Galatians 2:11) — public sin, public rebuke, equal standing."

"They withstood Uzziah the king (2 Chronicles 26:18) — eighty priests against a king at the height of his success."

"The prince of the kingdom of Persia withstood me one and twenty days (Daniel 10:13) — delay is not always refusal."
